newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan investors still prefer bonds to Tokyo stocks.
newsitem.headline: Japan investors still prefer bonds to Tokyo stocks.

text.p: Japanese institutional investors plan to increase the weighting of fixed-income bonds in their portfolios in January for a sixth consecutive month, but will keep trimming their holdings of Japanese equities, a Reuters investment survey showed on Friday.

In the survey, compiled this week, respondents altered their cautious attitudes towards securities markets after healthy adjustments in early December in the wake of comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan which invited temporary selling in global stock and bond markets.
Greenspan said on December 5 that the Fed must be wary when "irrational exuberance" infects stock and other asset markets, because that could end up doing damage to the economy.

In the survey, the average overall portfolio weighting of bonds rose for a sixth consecutive month, to 41.33 percent from 38.30 percent in the previous survey. It was the first time the weighting of bonds had topped 40 percent since July 1995.
The average overall weighting of equities was marginally higher at 46.25 percent against 45.80 percent in the previous survey.
The average overall weighting of cash holdings, however, fell 3.48 percentage points to 12.42 percent, the lowest weighting since March 1995.
The Reuters monthly Global Asset Allocation survey asked 16 Japan-based financial institutions about their recommended investment strategies for January.

Within the equities portfolio, the weighting in Japanese shares was lowered for the fourth consecutive month to 24.94 percent, down 4.17 percentage points from the previous survey and the lowest weighting since June 1994, when Reuters started its equities portfolio investment survey.
Respondents who lowered their weightings of Japanese equities said they did so because of a decline in confidence in Japan's economic recovery.

Many respondents pointed to scepticism over the government's optimistic outlook for the Japanese economy, saying the current weakness of the Tokyo stock market reflected suspicions about the government's policies.

"Demand and supply in the Japanese stock market is worse than expected. While internationally competitive blue-chip shares will be bought, other issues will remain under selling pressure," said an investment advisory company.
Meanwhile, the weighting of U.S. stocks was raised for the fourth consecutive month to 40.24 percent, up 1.81 percentage points from the previous survey.
An investment advisory firm said it expects an upward trend on Wall Street to continue for a while in the absence of negative factors.
Respondents said they felt there was little possibility of a credit tightening by the U.S. Federal Reserve in the first quarter of 1997.
